claim: Of 40 Alzheimer's risk genes, 30 (75%) had at least one annotated orthologue in the zebrafish genome.
source: Of these 40 Alzheimer's risk genes, 30 (75%) had at least one annotated orthologue in the zebrafish genome (source: Ensembl).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Ensembl database analysis of orthologues.

claim: 17 Alzheimer's risk genes had one orthologue in zebrafish.
source: Of those, 17 had one orthologue (e.g. the only zebrafish orthologue of human SORL1 was sorl1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: 11 Alzheimer's risk genes had two orthologues in zebrafish.
source: 11 had two orthologues (e.g. the zebrafish orthologues of human APP were appa and appb)
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: 2 Alzheimer's risk genes had more than two orthologues in zebrafish.
source: and 2 had more than two orthologues (e.g. the zebrafish orthologues of human MS4A6E included ms4a17a, ms4a17c.2, tmem176l, and more; Figure 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A human gene often has two or more zebrafish orthologues because of a teleost-specific whole-genome duplication event around 340 million years ago.
source: A human gene often has two or more zebrafish orthologues because of a teleost-specific whole-genome duplication event around 340 million years ago (Meyer and Málaga-Trillo, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There were no annotated orthologues for 10 Alzheimer's risk genes, including TREM2.
source: There were no annotated orthologues for 10 Alzheimer's risk genes, including TREM2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Ensembl database analysis.

claim: Most Alzheimer's risk gene orthologues (33/42) were detectable as early as 12 hr post-fertilisation in zebrafish embryos.
source: Most of the genes (33/42) were detectable as early as 12 hr post-fertilisation (hpf) and remained expressed throughout development (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: At 5 days post-fertilisation, 38 of the 42 orthologues (90%) were expressed in zebrafish.
source: At 5 days post-fertilisation (dpf), 38 of the 42 orthologues (90%) were expressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Zebrafish Psen1 is highly similar to human PSEN1 with ~70% identical amino acid sequence.
source: Zebrafish Psen1 and Psen2 are highly similar to their human counterparts (~70% identical amino acid sequence, Figure 3a and b)
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Zebrafish Psen2 is highly similar to human PSEN2 with ~70% identical amino acid sequence.
source: Zebrafish Psen1 and Psen2 are highly similar to their human counterparts (~70% identical amino acid sequence, Figure 3a and b)
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Zebrafish presenilins have the same critical amino acid at the four annotated active sites as human presenilins.
source: with the same critical amino acid at the four annotated active sites (two per presenilin).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Mismatches between human and zebrafish presenilins were largely clustered into disordered domains.
source: Mismatches between the human and zebrafish proteins were largely clustered into disordered domains, suggesting that the zebrafish presenilins have the same catalytic activity as in humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis and leads to an inference about catalytic activity.

claim: The zebrafish presenilins have the same catalytic activity as in humans.
source: Mismatches between the human and zebrafish proteins were largely clustered into disordered domains, suggesting that the zebrafish presenilins have the same catalytic activity as in humans.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the pattern of sequence mismatches.

claim: At each targeted locus of psen1, 99.0 ± 2.7% of reads had a small insertion and/or deletion (indel).
source: At each targeted locus of psen1, 99.0 ± 2.7% of reads had a small insertion and/or deletion (indel) and 78.6 ± 29.7% of all reads had a frameshift mutation (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina MiSeq sequencing data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: At each targeted locus of psen1, 78.6 ± 29.7% of all reads had a frameshift mutation.
source: At each targeted locus of psen1, 99.0 ± 2.7% of reads had a small insertion and/or deletion (indel) and 78.6 ± 29.7% of all reads had a frameshift mutation (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina MiSeq sequencing data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: At each targeted locus of psen2, 99.9 ± 0.1% reads had indels.
source: At each targeted locus of psen2, 99.9 ± 0.1% reads had indels and 82.0 ± 33.6% of all reads had a frameshift mutation (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina MiSeq sequencing data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: At each targeted locus of psen2, 82.0 ± 33.6% of all reads had a frameshift mutation.
source: At each targeted locus of psen2, 99.9 ± 0.1% reads had indels and 82.0 ± 33.6% of all reads had a frameshift mutation (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina MiSeq sequencing data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The biallelic knockout probability for psen1 and psen2 cumulatively reached >98%.
source: As each gene is mutated at three loci, the biallelic knockout probability, that is, the probability of having at least one frameshift mutation on both alleles, cumulatively reached >98% (francoiskroll.shinyapps.io/frameshiftmodel/), indicating that most psen1 and psen2 F0 knockout larvae were complete loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling based on the mutation data.

claim: Most psen1 and psen2 F0 knockout larvae were complete loss-of-function mutants.
source: As each gene is mutated at three loci, the biallelic knockout probability, that is, the probability of having at least one frameshift mutation on both alleles, cumulatively reached >98% (francoiskroll.shinyapps.io/frameshiftmodel/), indicating that most psen1 and psen2 F0 knockout larvae were complete loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high biallelic knockout probability.

claim: In humans, PSEN1 or PSEN2 acts as the catalytic subunit of the γ-secretase protein complex.
source: In humans, PSEN1 or PSEN2 acts as the catalytic subunit of the γ-secretase protein complex, which is responsible for the cleavage of more than 90 substrates, such as Notch.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: γ-secretase is responsible for the cleavage of more than 90 substrates, such as Notch.
source: In humans, PSEN1 or PSEN2 acts as the catalytic subunit of the γ-secretase protein complex, which is responsible for the cleavage of more than 90 substrates, such as Notch.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: γ-secretase performs the last cleavage of APP to release Aβ.
source: It also performs the last cleavage of APP to release Aβ, which aggregates in the brains of patients with AD (Haass and Selkoe, 1993; De Strooper et al., 1998; Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011; Kang et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Aβ aggregates in the brains of patients with AD.
source: It also performs the last cleavage of APP to release Aβ, which aggregates in the brains of patients with AD (Haass and Selkoe, 1993; De Strooper et al., 1998; Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011; Kang et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Aβ40 and Aβ42 were detectable in control (uninjected and scrambled-injected) zebrafish larvae.
source: Using a sensitive ELISA-based assay, Aβ40 and Aβ42 were detectable in control (uninjected and scrambled-injected) larvae but not in two clutches of psen1 F0 knockouts (Figure 3e)
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Aβ40 and Aβ42 were not detectable in two clutches of psen1 F0 knockouts.
source: Using a sensitive ELISA-based assay, Aβ40 and Aβ42 were detectable in control (uninjected and scrambled-injected) larvae but not in two clutches of psen1 F0 knockouts (Figure 3e)
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Zebrafish Psen1 is required for the cleavage of Appa/Appb into Aβ.
source: confirming that zebrafish Psen1 is required for the cleavage of Appa/Appb into Aβ.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the ELISA data showing no Aβ in psen1 knockouts.

claim: Aβ40 and Aβ42 were detectable in psen2 F0 knockouts.
source: In contrast, Aβ40 and Aβ42 were detectable in psen2 F0 knockouts, suggesting that most Aβ is generated by Psen1 in zebrafish and that Psen2 alone cannot compensate.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA assay data.

claim: Most Aβ is generated by Psen1 in zebrafish and Psen2 alone cannot compensate.
source: In contrast, Aβ40 and Aβ42 were detectable in psen2 F0 knockouts, suggesting that most Aβ is generated by Psen1 in zebrafish and that Psen2 alone cannot compensate.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the ELISA data showing Aβ in psen2 knockouts but not psen1 knockouts.

claim: Loss of PSEN2 had no measurable effect on Aβ40/42 production in mice.
source: This result extends previous findings that Aβ production in zebrafish is blocked by the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT (Özcan et al., 2022) and matches closely observations in mice, in which loss of PSEN2 had no measurable effect on Aβ40/42 production (Frånberg et al., 2011; Herreman et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on mice.

claim: Aβ production in zebrafish is blocked by the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT.
source: This result extends previous findings that Aβ production in zebrafish is blocked by the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT (Özcan et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In mice, knockout of Psen1, but not of Psen2, causes severe skeletal malformations and brain haemorrhages.
source: In mice, knockout of Psen1, but not of Psen2, causes severe skeletal malformations and brain haemorrhages, likely because of impaired Notch signalling (Herreman et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature on mice.

claim: Homozygous Psen1 knockout mice die within minutes after birth.
source: Homozygous animals die within minutes after birth (Shen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature on mice.

claim: psen1 F0 knockout zebrafish larvae developed normally and were indistinguishable from their wild-type siblings.
source: Morphologically, our psen1 F0 knockout larvae developed normally (tested up to 16 dpf) and were indistinguishable from their wild-type siblings, as observed in a psen1 stable knockout line (Sundvik et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations and a citation to published literature.

claim: psen2 F0 knockout larvae had a mild pigmentation defect.
source: psen2 F0 knockout larvae had a mild pigmentation defect (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a), which has been previously reported in a psen2 stable knockout line (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 3f and a citation to published literature.

claim: Psen2 has a specific function in melanophore development or function which cannot be fulfilled by Psen1.
source: This difference suggests a specific function of Psen2 in melanophore development or function which cannot be fulfilled by Psen1.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the pigmentation phenotype observed only in psen2 knockouts.

claim: Most psen1/psen2 double F0 knockouts were lethal early in development (~5 dpf) with severe defects in eye development.
source: We also generated psen1/psen2 double F0 knockouts but most were lethal early in development (~5 dpf) with severe defects in eye development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), in which the retinal pigment epithelium appeared patchy and some larvae developed oedema around the eye.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: psen1/psen2 double F0 knockout larvae had a severely curved tail outwards, in the same way as larvae treated with a high dose of the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT.
source: The tail was severely curved outwards, in exactly the same way as larvae treated with a high dose of the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations and a citation to published literature.

claim: Psen1 knockout mice display defects in the axial skeleton.
source: Incidentally, Psen1 knockout mice also display defects in the axial skeleton (Shen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature on mice.

claim: Zebrafish presenilins are more readily capable of compensating each other during development than in mice.
source: Overall, these results suggest that zebrafish presenilins are more readily capable of compensating each other during development than in mice, as only double psen1/psen2 knockout larvae showed a severe morphological phenotype.
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparing zebrafish and mouse phenotypes.

claim: At night, psen1 F0 knockout larvae slept slightly less (−8% vs. scrambled).
source: At night, psen1 F0 knockout larvae slept slightly less (−8% vs. scrambled, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: psen1 F0 knockout larvae spent more time active than control injected siblings at night (+22%).
source: and instead spent more time active than control injected siblings (+22%)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: psen1 F0 knockout larvae performed more swimming bouts at night (+20%) than controls.
source: mainly because they performed more swimming bouts (+20%).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: psen1 F0 knockouts showed a slightly reduced startle response at lights-off (−4%).
source: The psen1 knockouts also showed a slightly reduced startle response at lights-off (−4%), in line with some data obtained from stable psen1 knockout larvae (Sundvik et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data and a citation to published literature.

claim: Behaviour during the day was not affected in psen1 F0 knockouts.
source: Behaviour during the day was not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: psen2 F0 knockouts were substantially less active than controls during the day (total activity: −26% vs. scrambled).
source: In contrast, psen2 F0 knockouts of both clutches were substantially less active than controls during the day (total activity: −26% vs. scrambled, Figure 3g,h, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a,b)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in multiple figures.

claim: psen2 F0 knockouts performed fewer (−17%) and more subdued swimming bouts (active bout mean: −12%) during the day.
source: performing both fewer (−17%) and more subdued swimming bouts (active bout mean: −12%).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: psen2 F0 knockouts slept more during the day than controls, spending more time asleep (+178%) and initiating more frequent sleep bouts (+150%).
source: psen2 F0 knockouts also slept more during the day than controls (Figure 3g,h, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a,b), both spending more time asleep (+178%) and initiating more frequent sleep bouts (+150%).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Loss of Psen2 did not strongly affect night-time behaviour.
source: Loss of Psen2 did not strongly affect night-time behaviour.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: psen2 F0 knockout larvae were substantially less active and sleeping more than controls during the day.
source: In summary, psen2 F0 knockout larvae were substantially less active and sleeping more than controls during the day.
evidence: The claim is a summary of behavioral tracking data.

claim: psen2 F0 knockout larvae displaced fewer pixels during the startle response than scrambled-injected controls.
source: psen2 F0 knockout larvae indeed displaced fewer pixels during the startle response than scrambled-injected controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c, clutch 1: psen2 knockouts displaced 78 ± 10 pixels vs. 82 ± 8 pixels for scrambled-injected controls, clutch 2: 71 ± 8 pixels vs 80 ± 8 pixels).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Even after downscaling Δ pixel values to account for pigmentation differences, psen2 F0 knockouts were measurably less active and sleeping more during the day.
source: Even after this adjustment, psen2 F0 knockouts were measurably less active and sleeping more during the day, although the parameter effect sizes were somewhat reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data after correction shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3e.

claim: The psen2 behavioural phenotype reflects a genuine difference in behaviour.
source: In summary, the psen2 behavioural phenotype reflects a genuine difference in behaviour.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the analysis showing the phenotype persists after correction for pigmentation.

claim: Zebrafish Appa is highly similar to human APP (64–68% identical amino acid sequence).
source: As described previously (Özcan et al., 2022; Musa et al., 2001), zebrafish Appa and Appb are highly similar to human APP (64–68% identical amino acid sequence, Figure 3—figure supplement 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis and citations to published literature.

claim: Zebrafish Appb is highly similar to human APP (64–68% identical amino acid sequence).
source: As described previously (Özcan et al., 2022; Musa et al., 2001), zebrafish Appa and Appb are highly similar to human APP (64–68% identical amino acid sequence, Figure 3—figure supplement 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis and citations to published literature.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas9 RNPs used to generate appa/appb double F0 knockouts were highly mutagenic (across all four loci: 95.8 ± 7.0% mutated reads, 76.5 ± 21.7 of all reads had a frameshift mutation).
source: The CRISPR-Cas9 RNPs were highly mutagenic (across all four loci: 95.8 ± 7.0% mutated reads, 76.5 ± 21.7 of all reads had a frameshift mutation, Figure 3—figure supplement 4c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina MiSeq sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4c,d.

claim: appa/appb double F0 knockout larvae looked morphologically normal.
source: The appa/appb double F0 knockout larvae looked morphologically normal.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations.

claim: appa/appb double knockouts were less active during the day than control siblings (–14% vs. scrambled).
source: Behaviourally, appa/appb double knockouts were less active during the day than control siblings (–14% vs. scrambled, Figure 3—figure supplement 4e)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4e.

claim: appa/appb double knockouts showed shorter swimming bouts across the day/night cycle (active bout duration during the day: –4%; at night: –3%).
source: and showed shorter swimming bouts across the day/night cycle (active bout duration during the day: –4%; at night: –3%).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: Sleep was not consistently affected by the loss of appa/appb.
source: Sleep was not consistently affected by the loss of appa/appb (Figure 3—figure supplement 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4f.

claim: Knockout larvae for the three genes associated with early-onset AD had distinct morphological and behavioural phenotypes.
source: In summary, knockout larvae for the three genes associated with early-onset AD had distinct morphological and behavioural phenotypes, with the strongest behavioural changes observed for psen2 knockouts.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the morphological and behavioral data.

claim: Both presenilins are broadly expressed in the larval brain.
source: Since both presenilins are broadly expressed in the larval brain (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d), these results indicate that zebrafish Psen1- and Psen2-γ-secretases likely cleave different substrates
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d.

claim: Zebrafish Psen1- and Psen2-γ-secretases likely cleave different substrates.
source: these results indicate that zebrafish Psen1- and Psen2-γ-secretases likely cleave different substrates, such as Appa/Appb which is primarily cleaved into Aβ by Psen1-γ-secretase.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the distinct phenotypes and Aβ production data.

claim: Appa/Appb is primarily cleaved into Aβ by Psen1-γ-secretase.
source: such as Appa/Appb which is primarily cleaved into Aβ by Psen1-γ-secretase.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the Aβ production data showing no Aβ in psen1 knockouts but Aβ in psen2 knockouts.

claim: The behavioural phenotypes of appa/appb and psen1 knockout larvae had little overlap.
source: Moreover, the behavioural phenotypes of appa/appb and psen1 knockout larvae had little overlap while they presumably both resulted in the loss of Aβ.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing the behavioral data from both knockouts.

claim: The appa/appb day phenotype could be primarily caused by loss of some Appa/Appb cleavage product not relying on γ-secretase.
source: The appa/appb day phenotype could be primarily caused by loss of some Appa/Appb cleavage product not relying on γ-secretase.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the lack of phenotype overlap.

claim: The net effect of loss of all other Psen1-γ-secretase products could have masked the effect of loss of Aβ.
source: Alternatively, the net effect of loss of all other Psen1-γ-secretase products could have masked the effect of loss of Aβ.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the lack of phenotype overlap.

claim: APOE shares 22–25% amino acid identity with its two zebrafish orthologues, Apoea and Apoeb.
source: APOE shares 22–25% amino acid identity with its two zebrafish orthologues, Apoea and Apoeb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Double apoea/apoeb F0 knockout larvae performed slightly more subdued swimming bouts during the day than scrambled-injected siblings (active bout mean: −4%; active bout maximum: −5% vs. scrambled).
source: Consistently across three clutches, double apoea/apoeb F0 knockout larvae performed slightly more subdued swimming bouts during the day than scrambled-injected siblings (active bout mean: −4%; active bout maximum: −5% vs. scrambled; Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: At night, apoea/apoeb knockouts performed more swimming bouts (+31%) and had less sleep (−7%) than controls.
source: This slight hypoactivity is unlikely to reflect a motor defect because at night, apoea/apoeb knockouts performed more swimming bouts (+31%) and had less sleep (−7%, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) than controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Zebrafish cd2ap shares 44% identical amino acid sequence with human CD2AP.
source: We mutated zebrafish cd2ap (44% identical amino acid sequence vs. human CD2AP; Figure 4—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: cd2ap F0 knockouts were more active (time active: +38%; total activity: +44% vs. scrambled) and slept less at night than control siblings (−13%).
source: knockout larvae of both clutches were more active (time active: +38%; total activity: +44% vs. scrambled) and slept less at night than control siblings (−13%), mainly because they performed more swimming bouts (+34%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Zebrafish clu shares 39% identical amino acid sequence with human CLU.
source: Similarly, knockout of clu (39% identical amino acid sequence vs. human CLU, Figure 4—figure supplement 3a)
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Knockout of clu did not strongly affect behaviour during the day.
source: did not strongly affect behaviour during the day (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3c.

claim: At night, clu F0 knockouts were slightly more active (time active: +12% vs. scrambled) and slept less than control siblings (−7%).
source: At night, clu F0 knockouts were slightly more active (time active: +12% vs. scrambled) and slept less than control siblings (−7%, Figure 4—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Zebrafish sorl1 shares 63% identical amino acid sequence with human SORL1.
source: Finally, we generated F0 knockouts for sorl1 (63% identical amino acid sequence vs. human SORL1, Figure 4—figure supplement 4a)
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a.

claim: sorl1 F0 knockout larvae were less active during the day but slept less at night.
source: sorl1 F0 knockout larvae were less active during the day but slept less at night (Figure 4—figure supplement 5; Figure 4—figure supplements 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4c.

claim: During the day, sorl1 F0 knockouts spent less time active than scrambled-injected larvae (−15% vs. scrambled), performing fewer swimming bouts (−15%).
source: Specifically, during the day (Figure 4—figure supplement 4d), sorl1 F0 knockouts spent less time active than scrambled-injected larvae (−15% vs. scrambled), performing fewer swimming bouts (−15%) of approximately the same duration and intensity as controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4d.

claim: Sleep during the day was unaffected in sorl1 F0 knockouts.
source: Sleep during the day was unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: At night, sorl1 F0 knockouts spent more time active than control siblings (+20%), largely because their swimming bouts tended to last longer (+6%).
source: At night (Figure 4—figure supplement 4d), sorl1 F0 knockouts spent more time active than control siblings (+20%), largely because their swimming bouts tended to last longer (+6%).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4d.

claim: At night, sorl1 F0 knockouts slept less (−5%), initiating fewer sleep bouts (−9%) of roughly the same duration.
source: They also slept less (−5%), initiating fewer sleep bouts (−9%) of roughly the same duration.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: Loss of all four late-onset AD risk genes tested produced a fairly consistent phenotype at night, with all knockout larvae spending 5–13% less time asleep and instead spending 12–38% more time active because they were moving 13–34% more often.
source: Remarkably, loss of all four genes produced a fairly consistent phenotype at night (Figure 4), with all knockout larvae spending 5–13% less time asleep and instead spending 12–38% more time active because they were moving 13–34% more often.
evidence: The claim is a summary of behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each mutant of late-onset AD risk genes had distinct day-time behavioural alterations.
source: In contrast, each mutant had distinct day-time behavioural alterations.
evidence: The claim is a summary of behavioral tracking data.

claim: psen1 knockouts had similar night-time phenotypes to late-onset AD risk gene knockouts.
source: Comparing with early-onset genes, psen1 knockouts had similar night-time phenotypes, but knockout of psen2 or appa/appb had no effect on night-time sleep.
evidence: The claim is a summary of behavioral tracking data.

claim: Knockout of psen2 or appa/appb had no effect on night-time sleep.
source: but knockout of psen2 or appa/appb had no effect on night-time sleep.
evidence: The claim is a summary of behavioral tracking data.

claim: At least some late-onset (and one early-onset) Alzheimer's risk genes have common effects on sleep from an early age.
source: Therefore, at least some late-onset (and one early-onset) Alzheimer's risk genes have common effects on sleep from an early age, despite being expressed in different tissues and having distinct biochemical properties.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the behavioral data showing common night-time sleep phenotypes.

claim: Drugs used to treat depression are enriched at the top and/or bottom of the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints compared to the sorl1 knockout fingerprint (simulated p-value = 0.049).
source: More present among the small molecules most correlating and/or anti-correlating with the sorl1 fingerprint were drugs used to treat depression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, simulated p-value = 0.049)
evidence: The claim is supported by a permutation test on the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints.

claim: Drugs targeting the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 are enriched at the top and/or bottom of the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints compared to the sorl1 knockout fingerprint (simulated p-value = 0.015).
source: targeting the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 (Figure 5a and b, simulated p-value = 0.015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a permutation test on the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Drugs affecting the 'serotonergic synapse' pathway are enriched at the top and/or bottom of the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints compared to the sorl1 knockout fingerprint (simulated p-value = 0.027).
source: and affecting the 'serotonergic synapse' pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, simulated p-value = 0.027).
evidence: The claim is supported by a permutation test on the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: sorl1 knockout larvae behaved similarly to larvae treated with small molecules targeting serotonin signalling.
source: Thus, sorl1 knockout larvae behaved similarly to larvae treated with small molecules targeting serotonin signalling, suggesting that the loss of Sorl1 altered serotonin signalling.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the enrichment analysis.

claim: The loss of Sorl1 altered serotonin signalling.
source: Thus, sorl1 knockout larvae behaved similarly to larvae treated with small molecules targeting serotonin signalling, suggesting that the loss of Sorl1 altered serotonin signalling.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the enrichment analysis.

claim: At a low dose of citalopram (1 µM), sorl1 F0 knockouts and scrambled-injected controls reacted similarly, sleeping about 1.1 hr more during both day and night.
source: At a low dose of citalopram (1 µM, added directly to the fish water), sorl1 F0 knockouts and scrambled-injected controls reacted similarly, sleeping about 1.1 hr more during both day and night (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment shown in Figure 5c.

claim: At a higher dose of citalopram (10 µM), sorl1 F0 knockouts had a stronger reaction than their control siblings.
source: In contrast, at a higher dose of citalopram (10 µM), sorl1 F0 knockouts had a stronger reaction than their control siblings.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment.

claim: Sleep during the day increased 2.5× in sorl1 knockouts treated with 10 µM citalopram, while it only increased 2.2× in controls.
source: For example, sleep during the day increased 2.5× in sorl1 knockouts, while it only increased 2.2× in controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment.

claim: 10 μM citalopram displaced the sorl1 knockout larvae further from their behavioural baseline than it pushed controls from theirs.
source: Indeed, 10 μM citalopram displaced the sorl1 knockout larvae further from their behavioural baseline than it pushed controls from theirs.
evidence: The claim is supported by Euclidean distance analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: sorl1 F0 knockouts had a weaker reaction to fluvoxamine than their control siblings.
source: sorl1 F0 knockouts had a weaker reaction to fluvoxamine than their control siblings, the opposite effect than for citalopram.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment.

claim: Fluvoxamine doubled (2.1×) sleep bout length at night in sorl1 knockouts but tripled it (3.4×) in controls.
source: For example, fluvoxamine doubled (2.1×) sleep bout length at night in sorl1 knockouts but tripled it (3.4×) in controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: sorl1 knockout larvae reacted differently than control larvae to both SSRIs tested.
source: While it is surprising that the sorl1 knockout larvae reacted oppositely to the two SSRIs, they reacted differently than control larvae in both cases, demonstrating that our behavioural pharmacology approach correctly predicted from behaviour alone that serotonin signalling was in some way altered in sorl1 knockouts.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the drug treatment experiments.

claim: The behavioural pharmacology approach correctly predicted from behaviour alone that serotonin signalling was in some way altered in sorl1 knockouts.
source: demonstrating that our behavioural pharmacology approach correctly predicted from behaviour alone that serotonin signalling was in some way altered in sorl1 knockouts.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the differential drug responses.

claim: sorl1 F0 knockouts had slightly more (+2%) slc6a4a/b positive voxels than controls across regions.
source: sorl1 F0 knockouts had slightly more (+2%) slc6a4a/b positive voxels than controls across regions, but this difference was not definite for any one region and not replicated when looking at total signal intensity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by HCR quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1f.

claim: sorl1 F0 knockouts had on average 18% lower tph1a/1b/2 signal intensities across regions, particularly in the hypothalamus (hypothalamus – caudal zone 1: –24%).
source: sorl1 F0 knockouts had on average 18% lower tph1a/1b/2 signal intensities across regions, particularly in the hypothalamus (hypothalamus – caudal zone 1: –24%, Figure 5e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by HCR quantification data shown in Figure 5e and f.

claim: Of 94 clusters from the 5-dpf scRNA-seq dataset, sorl1 expression was highest in hypothalamic neurons enriched for tph1a expression.
source: Incidentally, of 94 clusters from the 5-dpf scRNA-seq dataset, sorl1 expression was highest in hypothalamic neurons enriched for tph1a expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SORL1 acts as an adaptor protein between retromer and several cargo proteins, such as APP.
source: SORL1 acts as an adaptor protein between retromer and several cargo proteins, such as APP (Jensen et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: SORL1 acts as an adaptor protein between retromer and GDNF receptor α1.
source: SORL1 acts as an adaptor protein between retromer and several cargo proteins, such as APP (Jensen et al., 2023), GDNF receptor α1 (Glerup et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: SORL1 acts as an adaptor protein between retromer and glutamate receptor 1 (GLUA1).
source: and glutamate receptor 1 (GLUA1; Mishra et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Retromer is a large protein complex which 'rescues' proteins from endosomes, targeting them to recycling instead of lysosomal digestion.
source: Retromer is a large protein complex which 'rescues' proteins from endosomes, targeting them to recycling instead of lysosomal digestion (Burd and Cullen, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: By disrupting retromer function, mutations in SORL1 disrupt endosomal recycling, which appears as swelling of early endosomes.
source: By disrupting retromer function, mutations in SORL1 disrupt endosomal recycling, which appears as swelling of early endosomes (Mishra et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: APP remains in endosomes for longer when SORL1 is mutated, where it is more likely to be cleaved by β-secretase, the first step towards production of Aβ.
source: As a result, APP remains in endosomes for longer, where it is more likely to be cleaved by β-secretase, the first step towards production of Aβ (Small and Petsko, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Retromer dysfunction lowers the level of GLUA1 receptors on the neuron membrane, likely because endocytosed receptors are not recycled back to the membrane.
source: Similarly, retromer dysfunction also lowers the level of GLUA1 receptors on the neuron membrane, likely because endocytosed receptors are not recycled back to the membrane, which can result in both increased or decreased firing rates in vitro (Mishra et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Some serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) receptors are recycled via retromer and SORL1.
source: We speculate that some serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) receptors are also recycled via retromer and SORL1.
evidence: The claim is speculation by the authors.

claim: sorl1 knockouts would react differently to a large spike in serotonin (SSRI treatment) as they have different levels of 5-HT receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
source: Consequently, sorl1 knockouts would react differently to a large spike in serotonin (SSRI treatment) as they have different levels of 5-HT receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
evidence: The claim is speculation by the authors.

claim: Both 5-HT type 4 receptor and SORL1 interact with sorting nexin 27, a subunit of retromer.
source: In support for this idea, both 5-HT type 4 receptor (Joubert et al., 2004) and SORL1 (Huang et al., 2016) interact with sorting nexin 27, a subunit of retromer.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 5-HT receptor type 4 was an enriched target for sorl1 (simulated p-value = 0.016).
source: Incidentally, the 5-HT receptor type 4 was also an enriched target for sorl1 (simulated p-value = 0.016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the permutation test on the ranked list of small molecule fingerprints.

claim: Treatment of an AD mouse model with citalopram caused a rapid decrease in Aβ concentrations in the ISF and eventually reduced amyloid plaque load.
source: For example, treatment of an AD mouse model with citalopram caused a rapid decrease in Aβ concentrations in the ISF and eventually reduced amyloid plaque load.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Humans treated with SSRIs within the past 5 years had significantly lower cortical amyloid plaque load on PET scans.
source: Additionally, humans treated with SSRIs within the past 5 years had significantly lower cortical amyloid plaque load on PET scans, suggesting a causal relationship (Cirrito et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Betamethasone completely resolved the excess day-time sleep of psen2 knockouts without causing hyperactivity.
source: Strikingly, betamethasone completely resolved the excess day-time sleep without causing hyperactivity (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Betamethasone rescued most, but not all, of the swimming bout alterations during both the day and night in psen2 knockouts (14/18 altered parameters rescued).
source: Betamethasone rescued most, but not all, of the swimming bout alterations during both the day and night (Figure 6c right, 14/18 altered parameters rescued).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Betamethasone caused a few side effects in psen2 knockouts, likely by making larvae overly aroused at the start of the night.
source: Betamethasone did cause a few side effects, likely by making psen2 knockout larvae overly aroused at the start of the night, extending sleep latency, steepening the slope in activity, and decreasing the startle response.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral tracking data with drug treatment and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Of the three drugs selected using behavioural pharmacology, one almost completely normalised the psen2 knockout phenotype, albeit with a few side effects.
source: Therefore, of the three drugs we selected using behavioural pharmacology, one almost completely normalised the psen2 knockout phenotype, albeit with a few side effects.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the drug treatment experiments.

claim: The F0 knockout and behavioural pharmacology approach successfully predicted the different sensitivity of sorl1 mutants to serotonin drugs.
source: The F0 knockout and behavioural pharmacology approach successfully predicted the different sensitivity of sorl1 mutants to serotonin drugs and identified a drug capable of normalising the psen2 knockout behavioural phenotype.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the results.

claim: The F0 knockout and behavioural pharmacology approach identified a drug capable of normalising the psen2 knockout behavioural phenotype.
source: The F0 knockout and behavioural pharmacology approach successfully predicted the different sensitivity of sorl1 mutants to serotonin drugs and identified a drug capable of normalising the psen2 knockout behavioural phenotype.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the results.

claim: Predictive behavioural pharmacology provides a generalisable framework that can be applied to any set of disease risk genes.
source: While we used genes associated with AD as a case study, predictive behavioural pharmacology provides a generalisable framework that can be applied to any set of disease risk genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: AD patients often take longer to fall asleep, have higher sleep fragmentation, and spend sharply less time in NREM sleep.
source: AD patients often take longer to fall asleep, have higher sleep fragmentation, and spend sharply less time in NREM sleep (D'Atri et al., 2021; Prinz et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sleep disruption can be present before the onset of cognitive deficits in AD.
source: Sleep disruption can be present before the onset of cognitive deficits.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Very high sleep fragmentation in elderly people is associated with subsequent diagnosis of AD.
source: For example, very high sleep fragmentation in elderly people is associated with subsequent diagnosis of AD (Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In healthy adults, one night of sleep deprivation was sufficient to cause a 25–30% increase in Aβ signal on PET scans.
source: In healthy adults, one night of sleep deprivation was sufficient to cause a 25–30% increase in Aβ signal on PET scans (Shokri-Kojori et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In healthy adults, one night of sleep deprivation caused a ~30% increase in CSF concentrations of Aβ.
source: a ~30% increase in CSF concentrations of Aβ (Lucey et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In healthy adults, one night of sleep deprivation caused a ~50% increase in CSF concentrations of tau.
source: and a ~50% increase in CSF concentrations of tau (Holth et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In wild-type rats and in mice overexpressing mutated human APP and PSEN1, restricting sleep for 21 days increased Aβ deposits in the cortex.
source: In wild-type rats and in mice overexpressing mutated human APP and PSEN1, restricting sleep for 21 days increased Aβ deposits in the cortex (Kang et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pharmaceutically or chemogenetically consolidating sleep in AD mouse models for 1–2 months delayed Aβ plaque formation.
source: Conversely, pharmaceutically or chemogenetically consolidating sleep in AD mouse models for 1–2 months delayed Aβ plaque formation (Kang et al., 2009; Jagirdar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disrupted sleep is likely to be a causal process in AD.
source: Disrupted sleep is therefore likely to be a causal process in AD.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental evidence on sleep and AD.

claim: An ongoing clinical trial (NCT04629547) is testing whether suvorexant can reduce Aβ accumulation by consolidating sleep in older adults without dementia.
source: An ongoing clinical trial (NCT04629547) is underway to test whether suvorexant, an orexin receptor antagonist that increases sleep, can reduce Aβ accumulation by consolidating sleep in older adults without dementia (Herring et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature about a clinical trial.

claim: Disruption of genes associated with AD diagnosis after 65 years reduces sleep in 7-day zebrafish larvae.
source: Our observation that disruption of genes associated with AD diagnosis after 65 years reduces sleep in 7-day zebrafish larvae suggest that disrupted sleep may be a common mechanism through which these genes exert an effect on risk.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the behavioral data.

claim: Disrupted sleep may be a common mechanism through which late-onset AD risk genes exert an effect on risk.
source: Our observation that disruption of genes associated with AD diagnosis after 65 years reduces sleep in 7-day zebrafish larvae suggest that disrupted sleep may be a common mechanism through which these genes exert an effect on risk.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: Impaired sleep early in life may be especially deleterious as it is likely essential for brain development.
source: Impaired sleep early in life may be especially deleterious as it is likely essential for brain development: infants spend most of their time asleep during the first year of life (Ednick et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by a citation about infant sleep patterns.

claim: Infants who carry the risk allele of APOE, ε4, show differences in grey matter volume and myelin content in multiple brain regions.
source: Incidentally, infants who carry the risk allele of APOE, ε4, show differences in grey matter volume and myelin content in multiple brain regions (Dean et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Differences in brain structure are present in children 9–17 years old who carry the disease-causing PSEN1 E280A mutation.
source: Differences are also present in children 9–17 years old who carry the disease-causing PSEN1 E280A mutation (Quiroz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In adults without dementia, higher genetic risk of AD correlate with some sleep phenotypes, sometimes as early as their early twenties.
source: In adults without dementia, higher genetic risk of AD correlate with some sleep phenotypes, sometimes as early as their early twenties (Chen et al., 2022; Leng et al., 2021; Muto et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The FramebyFrame R package extracts and analyses 17 behavioural parameters from frame-by-frame Δ pixel data.
source: The FramebyFrame package extracts and analyses 17 behavioural parameters from frame-by-frame Δ pixel data, which represent the number of pixels that changed intensity at each frame-to-frame transition.
evidence: The claim describes the functionality of the software developed in this study.

claim: The frame-by-frame analysis has several advantages over previous methods that analysed activity data at the 1-min resolution.
source: This frame-by-frame analysis has several advantages over previous methods that analysed activity data at the 1-min resolution (Rihel et al., 2010a; Lee et al., 2022; Rihel et al., 2010b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous methods cited.

claim: Individual swimming bouts could not be resolved by 1-min methods as single bouts last ~0.2 s on average.
source: First, individual swimming bouts could not be resolved by these methods as single bouts last ~0.2 s on average.
evidence: The claim is supported by data on bout duration.

claim: The 1-min methods missed around one third of all sleep bouts because of how the Δ pixel data is binned in 1-min epochs.
source: Second, the 1-min methods missed around one third of all sleep bouts because of how the Δ pixel data is binned in 1-min epochs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: During a sample 10 hr night, the frame-by-frame analysis detected 35 ± 14 more sleep bouts than the 1-min analysis.
source: For example, during a sample 10 hr night (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), the frame-by-frame analysis detected 35 ± 14 more sleep bouts
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The frame-by-frame analysis detected longer average sleep bout lengths (+0.2 ± 0.2 min) than the 1-min analysis.
source: longer average sleep bout lengths (+0.2 ± 0.2 min)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data.

claim: The frame-by-frame analysis detected shorter sleep latencies (1.6 ± 2.3 min earlier) than the 1-min analysis.
source: and shorter sleep latencies (1.6 ± 2.3 min earlier)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data.

claim: The frame-by-frame analysis resulted in a 42% increase in total sleep time (+2.3 ± 0.4 hr) compared to the 1-min analysis.
source: resulting in a 42% increase in total sleep time (+2.3 ± 0.4 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data.
